CR-SECURITY-05.corrected_title: The SSRF validator's synchronous DNS lookup blocks the single event loop for the whole resolver timeout on every unauthenticated /api/v1/url/* request (control route on the same loop starved 3.0s in an ASGI repro)
CR-SECURITY-05.known_status: new — no url_validator/event-loop row in M18 (`2026-09-01-m18-verified.json`: 0 matches for "url_validator") or M13 (`2026-08-31-m13-full-review.md`: 0 matches; its only `getaddrinfo` mention is test hygiene — "Patch socket.getaddrinfo in the three SSRF tests so they test the validator's logic rather than the internet", line 115). Neither offload set covers it (ENABLE_SYNC_DB_OFFLOAD = db_offload.run_db, ENABLE_ASYNC_REDIS_OFFLOAD = cache_service).
CR-SECURITY-05.reason: Reproduced through the runtime module, not by reading. Repro at scratchpad/m22-review/repro_cr_security_05.py (output repro_out.txt); url_validator.py and app/api/url_routes.py are byte-identical between 76ace90 and the working tree HEAD (git diff empty), so the evidence holds at the review SHA. (1) The defect is real and deterministic: with socket.getaddrinfo monkeypatched to a 3.0s resolver, calling validate_external_url from a coroutine let a 10ms ticker task advance 0 times in 3.000s (~300 expected) — the loop is fully stalled, and the stall length is the resolver's, not a constant. (2) It is service-wide, not per-request: mounting the REAL app.api.url_routes.router on FastAPI and driving it over httpx ASGITransport, a control GET /ping issued 200ms after GET /api/v1/url/detect returned only at t=3.204s. (3) It is unauthenticated: the router (url_routes.py:22) declares no dependencies and is mounted at main.py:177; a credential-free prod GET /api/v1/url/detect returned 200. THREE CORRECTIONS to the finding, none of which move severity. (a) The "validates url1 AND url2, doubling it" claim is WRONG for the stated blackhole attack: `not validate(url1) or not validate(url2)` short-circuits on the first False, and my repro counted exactly 1 getaddrinfo call for a compare whose resolver fails. Doubling needs url1 to resolve slowly-but-successfully. (b) Understated the other way: with a succeeding resolver the same compare made 6 getaddrinfo calls, because url_extraction_service.py:101 and :111 re-validate the initial URL and every redirect hop inside the async fetch — so the per-request blocking budget exceeds the 6 route-level sites the finder enumerated (same pattern at price_service.py:14126/14147 and shopify_pdp_service.py:284). (c) The file is app/api/url_routes.py, not app/routes/url_routes.py. MAGNITUDE IS THE WEAK PART OF THE EVIDENCE, so I did not upgrade: the 11.07s figure reproduces in kind on this box (13.15s for a nonexistent .example host) but the finder's "control resolve took 0.024s" did not — example.com took 7.02s here, i.e. this Windows resolver is slow across the board, and prod latency was unusable as evidence (this box saw 7.0s / 25.7s on plain /health). The seconds-per-request number on Railway's glibc resolver is MODELLED; the blocking itself is measured. Kept at P1, not P0: it needs an attacker, prod traffic is effectively zero and no user is harmed today; not below P1 because it is unauthenticated, single-worker, deterministic, and no shipped flag mitigates it. DOES THE PROPOSED FIX CLOSE IT? Yes — I transplanted it verbatim (asyncio.wait_for(loop.getaddrinfo(host, None), timeout=2.0), TimeoutError treated as blocked): against the same 3.0s resolver the ticker advanced 127 times and the call returned False at 1.998s. Two caveats to carry into the fix. wait_for abandons the future but cannot cancel the in-flight C call, so the resolver thread still parks for the full resolver timeout — and loop.getaddrinfo runs on the loop's DEFAULT executor, which since M13-34 is the shared sized `qaren-worker` pool (ADAPTER_EXECUTOR_MAX_WORKERS, default 40) also serving every M13-05/M13-06 to_thread offload, so a hostile flood converts loop starvation into pool contention with the DB/Redis offloads; give the resolve its own executor or a semaphore and state that interaction as the flag's precondition. Second, "keep a thin sync wrapper … that routes through asyncio.to_thread" is not implementable as written (to_thread is a coroutine, and the price_service/shopify_pdp/sitemap_discovery callers are themselves running inside executor threads) — those callers should keep the plain sync socket.getaddrinfo path. IS test_first THE RIGHT RED TEST? Yes in shape, and it is genuinely RED at HEAD — my node 1 is that test and it measures 0 ticks. Two hardening notes: add the node-2 assertion (drive the real router over ASGITransport and assert a concurrent control route is served during the validation) so a future refactor that awaits the validator but re-blocks in a helper still fails; and make the never-returns node use a stop-event-driven fake resolver, otherwise the abandoned non-daemon executor thread hangs the suite at teardown.

CR-SECURITY-04.corrected_title: verify_admin_key raises TypeError on any non-ASCII X-Admin-Key: one unauthenticated request 500s all 22 admin-key-gated routes and writes the plaintext ADMIN_API_KEY into Sentry frame vars
CR-SECURITY-04.known_status: new (not in M18/M13/mobile-checkup or the 33 open issues); composes with CR-SECURITY-03 (unscrubbed Sentry frame locals) and CR-SECURITY-11 (missing header -> 422). File unchanged 76ace90..HEAD 7dd04c1 (`git diff` on admin_routes.py / main.py / error_handler.py / history_routes.py is empty), so evidence holds at the brief's SHA.
CR-SECURITY-04.reason: Reproduced end-to-end through the real modules, not a lookalike; I could not break it. (1) Direct call of the real `app.api.admin_routes.verify_admin_key` (imported, sourcefile confirmed admin_routes.py:34): '\xff', 'eadmin' with acute-e, Arabic kaf, and the latin-1 view of UTF-8 'e-acute' ALL raise `TypeError: comparing strings with non-ASCII characters is not supported`, while '' and 'wrong' raise the intended HTTPException 403 and the correct key returns True - so the fault is specifically the non-ASCII byte, exactly as claimed. (2) Escalation confirmed through the WHOLE app: `TestClient(app.main.app, raise_server_exceptions=False).get('/api/v1/admin/stats/daily', headers={'X-Admin-Key': b'\xff'})` returns HTTP 500 SERVER_ERROR (ErrorHandlerMiddleware, error_handler.py:135-160), versus 403 for a wrong ASCII key and 200 for the correct one - unauthenticated, no rate-limit reached, no auth required. The CR-SECURITY-11 sub-claim also reproduced: omitting the header entirely gives 422, not 403. (3) The credential half is MEASURED, not modelled: I re-ran the raise under a real `sentry_sdk.init(...)` wired with the repo's own `app.services.sentry_service._before_send`, send_default_pii=False, and a local stub transport (no network, nothing sent to the real project) - the serialized event contains the plaintext ADMIN_API_KEY, in frame vars `{"x_admin_key": "'\xff'", "expected": "'SUPER_SECRET_PROD_ADMIN_KEY_123'"}` at admin_routes.py:37. My best break-attempt was that `_before_send` would scrub it: it does not - it scrubs exception values, breadcrumbs, request headers (incl. x-admin-key) and query strings, but never `stacktrace.frames[].vars`, and `sentry_sdk.init` at sentry_service.py:215 never passes `include_local_variables` (SDK default True, verified). SENTRY_DSN IS present in the prod Railway `web` var list, so the channel is live. Two corrections: the route count is 22 (`Depends(verify_admin_key)` = 19 in admin_routes.py + 3 in text_routes.py), not the 17/19 the finder gave; and the header-decode step is off-lock locally (starlette 0.38.6 vs lock 1.6.0) - latin-1 header decoding is ASGI-spec behaviour and `hmac.compare_digest`'s ASCII restriction is CPython stdlib, so I judge both version-independent, but the TestClient 500 itself is "local, off-lock". Kept at P1 rather than upgraded: the DoS reaches only internal admin routes (no user-facing flow), and the leaked key lands in the owner's own Sentry project, which the attacker cannot read - disclosure to a third-party store, not to the attacker. DOES THE PROPOSED FIX CLOSE MY REPRO: yes, measured. Re-running all seven cases through `hmac.compare_digest(x.encode('utf-8','ignore'), expected.encode('utf-8'))` yields 403 for every non-ASCII case, for '' and for 'wrong', and True only for the correct key - zero TypeErrors. Two notes: `.encode('latin-1','ignore')` would round-trip the actual wire bytes more faithfully than utf-8 (utf-8 re-encodes the latin-1-decoded string, so a non-ASCII ADMIN_API_KEY could never be matched byte-exactly), but since it fails closed to 403 either way and the key is ASCII in practice this is a refinement, not a defect; and the `Header(default="")` half of the fix is genuinely required - I measured the 422, so without it a missing header still bypasses the 403 path. The fix must ship with CR-SECURITY-03's `include_local_variables=False` as the finder says, since the byte-safe compare alone leaves every OTHER raising frame's locals exposed. IS test_first THE RIGHT RED TEST: yes, and it is RED today - the parametrised `verify_admin_key` cases raise TypeError instead of HTTPException(403), and the TestClient case returns 500 instead of 403. Two refinements I would make: '' in the parametrise list only exercises the direct-call path (a genuinely missing header 422s before the dependency body runs), so add an explicit missing-header case asserting 403-not-422; and add a third assertion using the stub-transport pattern I ran - capture the Sentry event and assert `ADMIN_API_KEY not in json.dumps(event)` - otherwise the test pins only the availability half and a future regression that re-enables local variables would slip through silently.

CR-PERFORMANCE-01.corrected_title: extract_price_from_html parses the same html with BeautifulSoup 4x per call on 89/92 cached PDPs — measured 363 soups for 92 pages; sharing one parse cuts 67% of its blocking event-loop CPU with byte-identical results
CR-PERFORMANCE-01.reason: Reproduced independently with my own harness (not the finder's m_soup.py), and the defect manifests exactly as claimed. Cited lines are verbatim at HEAD 76ace90: 10642 and 13056 are both `soup = BeautifulSoup(html, 'html.parser')`; 13092/13097/13112 are the three `extract_jsonld_price(` calls on the SAME `html` string. Counting bs4.BeautifulSoup.__init__ over the 10 largest cached _proof/html PDPs reproduced the finder's headline number to the digit: soups=4 on every page, 40 total, 17,110,052 bytes parsed for 4,277,513 bytes of input (4.00x), 1,991 ms. I then attacked the two ways this could have been an artifact of an unrealistic query, and both attacks failed to break it: (a) with a *matching* query — each of the 92 cached PDPs >20 KB queried with its own JSON-LD/og name, 17 of which actually yield a price — the count is still 4 soups on 89/92 pages (hist {2:2, 3:1, 4:89}, 363 soups total, 24,621 ms, median 149.5 ms/page, p95 771 ms), so the 4x is the normal case, not the miss case; a first-pass JSON-LD hit still costs 2 parses because 13056 always runs before the ladder. (b) The blocking claim holds: all four runtime call sites are INLINE (no to_thread/run_in_executor) inside `async def` — price_service.py:14090 in `async def fetch_page_price` (14060), structured_comparison_service.py:1643 in `async def _firecrawl_scraper` (1599), :1722 in `async def _scrapedo_scraper` (1674), and :2879 in `async def _fetch_page_price` (2871). ENABLE_PAGE_SCRAPE=true in the captured Railway `web` vars, and `jsonld_first_enabled()` measured True with no env override (so the third pass at 13112 does run in prod); `not_a_pdp_filter_enabled()` measured False, so its extra soup consumer is not even the cause. DOES THE PROPOSED FIX CLOSE IT — yes, and I measured it rather than reasoning about it. Without editing any tracked file I emulated "parse once and thread the soup through" by swapping `bs4.BeautifulSoup` for a memoizing factory that returns the same soup object for the same markup within one call (exactly the sharing set the fix creates: outer soup + the three ladder calls). Over all 92 pages: 363 -> 92 soups (1 per page), 24,621 ms -> 8,239 ms, saved 16,383 ms (67%), and `result_diffs=0` — every returned price dict JSON-identical to HEAD, including all 17 hits. So the fix's "byte-identical by construction" claim is empirically supported, not just asserted; the soup= default-None signature also means no call site outside the file changes, and the optional ENABLE_SHARED_SOUP_PARSE gate is a reasonable belt-and-braces. IS test_first THE RIGHT RED TEST — yes, verbatim. I built the exact fixture it describes (a page whose JSON-LD Product has no matching offer, so all three ladder passes run), monkeypatched the bs4 constructor with a counter, and got: HEAD soups=4 result=None; with the parse shared soups=1 result=None. So `assert counter == 1` is RED today at 4 and GREEN under the fix, with the return value unchanged — it pins the defect and nothing else. One caveat worth writing into the test: assert ==1 only for a no-match fixture (a hit path can legitimately build additional soups elsewhere in the cascade). TWO CORRECTIONS that do not change severity: (1) the finder's "~75% of that (~1.9 s)" overstates the recoverable share — I measure 62% on the 10-page sample and 67% on the full 92, i.e. ~16.4 s of 24.6 s, not 75%; I did not reproduce the "bs4.__init__ cumtime 4.286 s = 88.6%" cProfile figure and treat the wall-clock delta as the load-bearing number instead. (2) The impact paragraph's causal attribution of the 1,288 "Still gathering prices" + 209 "couldn't finish in time" search_logs rows to THIS defect is unproven and I would strike it — the brief states recent failures are the OpenAI/Serper outage, and nothing links those rows to soup parsing. Severity: keeping P1 rather than dropping to P2. It is not a correctness bug and prod traffic is currently ~zero (16 requests/24h), so no user is harmed today — that is the honest case for P2. But it is a defect reachable by users on the live compare path the moment there is traffic: ~150 ms median and up to 771 ms p95 of *blocking* CPU per candidate page on a single-worker uvicorn loop, two-thirds of it pure duplicate work, multiplied by N Tier-1.5 candidates inside a 15 s price race and a 30 s STREAM_HARD_CAP, and it stalls unrelated concurrent requests exactly like the M18/M13 loop-blocking family (#71/#73/M13-05) that was rated P1. It is also the cheapest P1 in the pile: measured 67% recovery, zero output change, one optional parameter.
